tldr: We propose a method that combines simulation motion generation by coding agents with photorealistic rendering via a video generation model fine-tuned on paired data, synthesizing large volumes of photorealistic robot training data with accurate action labels without human demonstration collection.

(c) In new environments, the agent automatically writes task code and executes it in simulation; the renderer then translates these runs into photorealistic videos, synthesizing demonstration data with aligned action labels.
overview:
Scaling robot learning requires large quantities of visual data with realistic appearance alongside accurate action labels. However, collecting data via human teleoperation demands immense effort and cost. On the other hand, while simulation-based data synthesis offers high scalability, it suffers from a severe Sim-to-Real visual gap. Conversely, relying solely on video generation models leads to a dilemma: physical contacts often break down, and accurate action labels are missing.

To address this, the authors decouple physical interaction generation from appearance rendering. Specifically, an LLM-based coding agent (GPT-6 Astra) automatically builds corresponding simulation environments from existing real-world robot data, constructing a paired dataset of real-world and simulator videos. A video diffusion model is fine-tuned on these pairs, training a renderer conditioned on proxy videos (coarse simulation footage) and reference images to translate them into photorealistic video. For new environments and tasks, the agent reconstructs the scene geometry, writes task execution code, and executes it in simulation while randomizing object layouts. By passing the resulting proxy videos through the renderer, the framework automatically generates demonstration data that unites simulator-derived, ground-truth action labels with photorealistic visuals.

In real-robot evaluations on a bimanual platform across three tasks (block stacking, can-in-tray, and pen insertion), policies trained solely on the generated data outperformed raw simulation training by over 30 percentage points and approached the performance of training on an equal number of real-world demonstrations. Furthermore, performance scaled with increasing amounts of generated data, and the per-demonstration cost in mass production was substantially lower than human teleoperation.
contributions: Proposed DemoFoundry, an automated data engine that couples coding-agent-based motion program generation with generative rendering to automatically synthesize photorealistic robot demonstrations with accurate action labels without human intervention.
Automatically constructed an aligned real–proxy video pair dataset comprising 1,884 episodes (1,522 total minutes) from four public robot datasets through iterative agent-driven refinement.
Significantly improved visual fidelity as well as temporal and physical action–video consistency by adapting state-of-the-art video generation models on paired data.

Demonstrated on three bimanual real-robot manipulation tasks that policy learning using generated data vastly outperforms raw simulation and achieves success rates comparable to real-world demonstrations.

sections.heading: From human demonstrations to automated synthesis via code and video generation
sections.summary: Scaling robot learning requires both high-quality visual observations and accurate action labels, but human teleoperation is prohibitively expensive. This work introduces DemoFoundry, fully automating the synthesis of photorealistic demonstration data by coupling coding agents for control program generation with generative video rendering.
sections.details:
Training generalist robot policies requires large-scale data that covers diverse environments and object interactions. However, collecting data through human teleoperation requires continuous manual effort not only for task execution but also for scene resetting, creating a major bottleneck for scaling data collection.

While physics simulators can mass-produce data safely and quickly, they suffer from a substantial Sim-to-Real gap, as object textures, lighting, and backgrounds diverge sharply from real environments. Meanwhile, although recent video generation models can produce realistic visual scenes, physical consistency in object contact and motion tends to collapse. Crucially, they cannot provide the precise action labels (joint positions or velocities) required to drive the robot. Inferring actions from videos via inverse dynamics introduces additional estimation errors.

To tackle this, this work focuses on decoupling physical interaction generation from appearance synthesis. Executable programs generate reliable action logs and coarse simulation footage (proxy videos), which a video renderer then translates into photorealistic observations. By automating this entire pipeline—paired data construction, novel-scene geometry reconstruction, task code authoring, and generative rendering—with coding agents, the authors developed DemoFoundry to synthesize photorealistic robot data without human intervention.

sections.heading: Fusing program-driven simulation with generative rendering
sections.summary: Prior work was divided across programmatic simulation generation, digital twin reconstruction of real environments, and visual translation via video generation models. DemoFoundry comprehensively advances these directions: an agent constructs paired data from real episodes to train a renderer, and also writes code for novel tasks.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Program-Driven Simulation and Data Engines
Research using LLMs to automatically generate executable robot control code and task specifications (such as RoboTwin 2.0 and Genie Sim) has been actively progressing. While effective for expanding motion diversity, their visual outputs remain confined to simulator-level appearances. DemoFoundry extends this paradigm by connecting generated motion proxies directly to a video renderer for photorealistic translation.

### 2.2 Robot Data Synthesis from Real Observations
Real-to-Sim approaches reuse trajectories from real demonstrations or reconstruct 3D digital twins of physical environments in simulators. However, manually building detailed assets for individual scenes is labor-intensive. In DemoFoundry, agents automatically extract correspondences between real robots and simulators across multiple existing datasets, utilizing them as paired training data for a generalist video renderer.

### 2.3 Generative Rendering for Robot Learning
Methods such as DreamGen recover actions from video generation models via inverse dynamics, while others like RoboRender and Cosmos-Transfer guide photorealistic rendering using geometric cues such as depth and segmentation masks. However, strict synchronization between actions and video, as well as zero-shot adaptation to novel scenes, remain challenging. DemoFoundry establishes a systematic, automated pipeline by coupling multi-source paired data construction by agents directly with task programming.

sections.heading: How agents write code and renderers synthesize photorealism
sections.summary: The system builds pairs of real and proxy videos from existing data to train a video renderer. For novel tasks, an agent sets up the simulator environment and writes control programs; the resulting proxy videos are rendered into photorealistic demonstrations with aligned action labels.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Overview and Formulation
DemoFoundry operates in two main stages. First, it automatically constructs pairs of real-world videos and simulated proxy videos from existing real robot datasets to train a conditional video renderer. Next, given a reference image $I^{\mathrm{ref}}$ of a novel scene, robot specifications $R$, camera calibration $C$, and a task instruction $\ell$, an agent generates a simulation environment $E$ and a task program $p$. Executing this program yields proxy videos $P$, robot state sequences $Q$, and action sequences $A$. The renderer $G_\theta$ then translates $P$ into photorealistic observations $\widehat{V}$, producing training data $(\widehat{V}, Q, A, \ell)$.

### 3.2 Training the Video Renderer
To build the paired training dataset, four public datasets are used: DROID, AgiBot World, RoboMIND, and RH20T. The GPT-6 Astra agent extracts object masks from RGB-D and camera metadata using SAM 3.1, and reconstructs 3D assets using SAM 3D Objects and Blender scripts. The reconstructed assets and robot models are loaded into a physics engine like MuJoCo to replay the recorded actions.
A crucial component here is the automated alignment verification loop. The agent compares object silhouette IoU across keyframes and refines object scales and initial poses up to three times until the IoU reaches 0.80 or higher across all camera views. This process produced an aligned dataset of 1,884 pairs totaling 1,522 minutes. Using these pairs, pretrained video generation models (LTX-2.5 and MiniMax-H3) are fine-tuned via LoRA under a Flow Matching formulation.

### 3.3 Novel Scene Demonstration Generation and Policy Learning
In an unseen scene, the agent reconstructs objects from reference images, places them in the simulator, and authors a task program $p$ using a tool library $\mathcal{T}$ containing kinematics solvers and grasp proposers. The program executes in simulation with randomized object poses, collecting only successful episodes. An image generation model $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{img}}$ (such as Qwen-Image-2.1) generates a reference image $I_i^{\mathrm{ref}}$ matching the initial object layout, and the video renderer translates the proxy videos into photorealistic footage $\widehat{V}_i$. For long-horizon trajectories, generation unrolls autoregressively with a 1-frame overlap across clip windows. The synthesized data is then used to train policies such as Diffusion Policy and $\pi_{0.5}$.

sections.heading: Real-robot validation: Real-level performance and striking cost efficiency
sections.summary: The proposed renderer outperformed existing video generation baselines in both visual fidelity and action consistency. In real bimanual robot experiments across three tasks, policies trained purely on generated data substantially surpassed raw simulation and approached the success rates of real-world demonstrations.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Implementation and Experimental Setup
Two fine-tuned renderers were evaluated: an LTX-2.5-based model (Ours LTX) and a MiniMax-H3-based model (Ours H3). Downstream policies included Diffusion Policy (DP) and the VLA model $\pi_{0.5}$. Real-robot evaluations were conducted on a TianJi bimanual robot (Marvin M6S) across three tasks: can-in-tray, block stacking, and pen insertion (30 trials each).

### 4.2 Visual Fidelity and Action–Video Consistency
In visual quality benchmarks on the test set, Ours (H3) outperformed baselines such as Cosmos-Transfer and Wan2.2 across all metrics: PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, and FVD. Compared to raw MiniMax-H3, PSNR improved by 7.86 dB and FVD decreased by 68.0%. In addition, Ours (H3) achieved an outstanding 95.23% in EventAlign (contact timing consistency within ±0.5 s) alongside high PCK for robot end-effector and object tracking.

### 4.3 Real-Robot Policy Learning Results
In real-robot experiments using 50 episodes per task, the average success rate across all three tasks for policies trained purely on generated data (DemoFoundry-only) exceeded raw simulation (Simulation-only) by 34.4 points for DP and 32.2 points for $\pi_{0.5}$. Furthermore, adding 100 generated demonstrations to 50 real demonstrations boosted average success rates by 23.3 points for DP and 20.0 points for $\pi_{0.5}$ over real demonstrations alone. In contrast, adding raw simulation data yielded almost no improvement, demonstrating the necessity of photorealistic rendering.

### 4.4 Ablations, Scaling, and Cost Analysis
Removing paired-data fine-tuning for the renderer resulted in a 15.6-point drop in policy success rate. Scaling generated demonstrations from 25 to 200 consistently improved the average success rate of $\pi_{0.5}$ from 42.2% to 85.6%. In terms of cost, amortizing the initial program generation cost by GPT-6 Astra (approx. $9) over multiple episodes brings the per-demo cost down to $0.855 for 100 demonstrations and $0.774 for 1,000 demonstrations—less than one-third of the cost of human teleoperation (approx. $2.42 per demo).

sections.heading: Summary and future directions
sections.summary: DemoFoundry integrates coding agents and generative rendering to automatically generate robot demonstrations that balance physical consistency with photorealism. Future work will address multi-view geometric consistency and long-horizon drift.
sections.details:
This paper presented DemoFoundry, an automated data engine fusing the programmatic authoring capabilities of coding agents with the expressive power of video generation models. Through real-robot evaluations, it proved high visual fidelity and precise action alignment, showing strong promise for drastically reducing manual demonstration collection in real-robot policy training.

Current limitations include slight cross-view texture discrepancies because multiple cameras (such as head and wrist views) are rendered independently, as well as gradual drift over long-horizon autoregressive unrolling. Future improvements are expected through the adoption of multi-view joint generation models and memory mechanisms that reference past frames.

sections.heading: Appendix: Agent feedback loops and visual domain randomization
sections.summary: The appendix details how the agent self-refines programs based on execution errors and mask alignment, and presents evaluation results on strong visual domain randomization via prompt editing.
sections.details:
### Agent Feedback Design
Appendix A details the tool library $\mathcal{T}$ and verification loop used by the agent (GPT-6 Astra). In the alignment check, if the object silhouette IoU at keyframes is below 0.80, feedback is provided to the agent to adjust asset scale and initial placement. Through iterative refinement, the paired data pass rate increased from an initial 33.1% to 39.7%, and center-of-mass tracking error dropped from 1.370% to 0.956%.

### Domain Randomization via Prompts
Appendix C shows that editing the video renderer's text prompt enables arbitrary variations in object colors, backgrounds, and lighting conditions. Compared to traditional manual domain randomization in simulation (Simulation + DR), which achieved only a 2/30 success rate under unseen lighting, policies trained on DemoFoundry data achieved 18/30 success, demonstrating superior robustness.

takeaways: Decoupling physical motion generation (simulator + code) from appearance synthesis (video generative renderer) is highly effective for combining accurate action labels with photorealism.

When applying video diffusion models to robot control, aligning and fine-tuning on real–proxy paired video data via LoRA is critical for preserving physical consistency and achieving high policy success rates.
Changing only text prompts enables photorealistic visual domain randomization for lighting and textures, eliminating the need to build complex material and lighting setups in simulators.
limitations: Multiple camera viewpoints, such as head and wrist cameras, are rendered independently, meaning strict 3D consistency across views is not fully guaranteed.
When stitching video clips autoregressively for long-horizon tasks, there is a risk of gradual visual drift in object appearance and background details.
The approach has limited applicability to tasks with highly intricate contact dynamics or deformable objects where code-based motion generation in simulation fails.
